title: Synonyms & Antonyms
summary: One synonym and one antonym in a typical Tier 1 shift — two fast marks that reward a word bank, not guesswork. The root-word method decodes unknown words; degree and charge matching settle the rest. Below: 100 high-frequency synonyms and 60 antonyms with meanings, written for revision in daily 15-minute doses.

subtopics.title: The root-word method: decode words you have never seen
subtopics.concept:
SSC vocabulary questions recycle the same few thousand words, but every year a couple of words are new to almost everyone. The root-word method converts such words from guesses into deductions: most English 'hard' words are built from Latin and Greek parts, and knowing 40 roots covers hundreds of exam words.

| Root | Sense | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| bene- | good, well | benevolent, benefit, benign, benefactor |
| mal-/male- | bad | malevolent, malice, malfunction, malnutrition |
| bon-/eu- | good | bona fide, euphoria, eulogy |
| loqu / locut | speak | eloquent, loquacious, elocution, soliloquy |
| dict | say, declare | dictate, contradict, verdict, predict |
| voc / vok | call, voice | vocal, revoke, advocate, invoke |
| cred | believe | credible, credulous, incredible, credit |
| mit / miss | send | transmit, emissary, remit, missile |
| path | feeling, suffering | sympathy, apathy, empathy, pathological |
| sens / sent | feel | sensitive, sentiment, consensus, dissent |
| morph | shape, form | amorphous, metamorphosis, morpheme |
| chron | time | chronic, chronology, synchronise, anachronism |
| temp | time | temporary, contemporary, temporal |
| ego | self | egocentric, egoist, alter ego |
| ambi / amphi | both, around | ambiguous, ambidextrous, amphibious |
| am / amic | love, friend | amiable, amicable, amity, amorous |
| anthrop | human | anthropology, philanthropy, misanthrope |
| phil | love | philanthropy, philosopher, bibliophile |
| phob | fear | phobia, hydrophobia, acrophobia |
| gen | birth, kind | genius, generate, genocide, congenital |
| graph / scrib / script | write | autograph, describe, manuscript, scribble |
| spec / spect | look | inspect, spectator, circumspect, perspective |
| vis / vid | see | visible, evident, vision, provident |
| aud | hear | audible, audience, auditorium |
| port | carry | transport, portable, export, deport |
| duc / duct | lead | conduct, educate, deduce, aqueduct |
|  tract | pull, draw | attract, extract, retract, tractable |
| press | press, push | compress, depress, impression |
| pos / pon | place | position, postpone, deposit, component |
| sequ / secut | follow | sequence, consequence, execute, sequel |
| cert | sure | certain, certify, ascertain |
| cur / curs | run | current, excursion, cursory, cursive |
| rupt | break | rupture, interrupt, bankrupt, erupt |
| fid | faith | confide, fidelity, diffident, confident |
| greg | flock, group | gregarious, segregate, aggregate |
| jur / jud | law, judge | jury, justice, prejudice, adjudicate |
| leg / lex | law, read | legal, legislate, legacy, lexicon |
| sol | alone / sun | solitude, solitary, solo / solar, solstice |
| ver | truth | verify, veracity, verdict, veritable |
| grad / gress | step, go | gradual, progress, digress, egress |

**How to deploy it in the exam.** When you meet an unknown word, split it:
- *MALEVOLENT* = male- (bad) + vol (wish) + -ent → 'wishing bad' → hostile. Even without recalling *vol*, 'male-' alone rules out friendly options.
- *CIRCUMSPECT* = circum- (around) + spect (look) → 'looking around' → cautious.
- *SOLILOQUY* = soli (alone) + loqu (speak) → 'speaking alone' → a monologue.

Prefixes and suffixes also reveal the part of speech even when meaning stays dark: *-ous/-ful* build adjectives (*dangerous*), *-tion/-ment* build nouns (*creation*), *-ise/-fy* build verbs (*simplify*). Knowing the class alone eliminates two of four options in synonym questions, because options usually mix classes.

**Build the habit:** whenever you learn a new word, spend ten seconds finding its root. The root then pays out on every relative of that word — learn *credulous* and *incredible, credible, creed, credential* all come free.

tricks.title: Split-then-eliminate
tricks.body: Chop the unknown word at its joins (bene-vol-ent), translate the parts you know, and eliminate options contradicting them. One confident root kills two options.

example.q: BENEVOLENT means: cruel / kindly / generous-sized / talkative.
example.solution: *Bene-* = good → the kind option. *Malevolent* (male- = bad) would be the antonym — options often plant it as a decoy.

tricks.title: Family clustering
tricks.body: Learn words in root families, not alphabetical order: dict family (dictate, verdict, indomitable? no — edict, indict), loqu family (eloquent, loquacious). One sitting per family.

tricks.title: Positive/negative split
tricks.body: Roots carry emotional charge: bene-, eu-, am- are warm; mal-, dys-, phob-, mis- are cold. When stuck, mark the word's charge and choose an option of matching charge.

mistakes: Trusting the first familiar half ('understand' contains 'stand' but is not about standing).
Ignoring suffixes and losing the part-of-speech elimination.
Learning alphabetical lists; root families stick, alphabet lists evaporate.

subtopics.title: Choosing the nearest meaning: elimination by class, degree, charge
subtopics.concept:
A synonym question asks for the word closest in meaning. Options are engineered around three axes — fix them in order:

**1. Part of speech.** Decide whether the given word is a noun, verb or adjective; options that are not the same class are out immediately. *AFFECT* (verb) cannot have 'affection' (noun) as a synonym even though it looks closest.

**2. Degree.** The nearest synonym matches the *intensity*. *WEARY* (very tired) is closer to *exhausted* than to *tired*; *FUTILE* (completely fruitless) is closer to *pointless* than to *difficult*. When two options both fit, take the one at the same temperature.

**3. Connotation and register.** A word's emotional colour must match. *NOTORIOUS* (famous for bad reasons) pairs with *infamous*, not with *celebrated*, even though both mean 'widely known'. *SLIM* and *skinny* both mean thin, but *slim* is approving and *skinny* is not — synonym options are chosen across this line.

**Practical routine for 20 seconds:**
1. Say the given word's meaning in your own simple words.
2. Translate each option into its own simple meaning.
3. Keep the option whose simple meaning overlaps most — overlap, not association. (*Cinema* associates with *film* but is not its synonym.)

**No sentence is given in SSC's format** — so context cannot rescue you. This is the one topic where the answer must be known, which is exactly why the word banks in this topic deserve daily 15-minute revision rather than a single reading.

tricks.title: Overlap test
tricks.body: The right synonym shares the core idea, not the neighbourhood. Ask 'can one replace the other in most sentences?' — if the sentence changes meaning, it is an associate, not a synonym.

example.solution: *Eloquent* = speaking fluently and movingly = **articulate**. 'Quiet' is a near-antonym planted for sound-alike confusion.

tricks.title: Charge matching
tricks.body: Label the given word + or − (notorious −, celebrated +) and pick the option of the same sign. Half of synonym options fall to charge alone.

tricks.title: Degree ruler
tricks.body: Place the word and both surviving options on an intensity line (mild → extreme). The option at the same mark is the answer.

mistakes: Choosing the option that merely sounds academic ('utilise' is fine, but 'effectuate' for 'do' is not SSC's style).
Picking a word of the wrong part of speech that shares a root with the answer.
Forgetting the negative flip: 'famous for good deeds' ≠ notorious.

subtopics.title: Antonyms: prefix flips and real opposites
subtopics.concept:
An antonym is a word opposite in meaning. Two skills cover SSC antonym questions.

**Skill 1 — the opposite, not the absence.** The correct antonym reverses the meaning; it does not merely differ. For *BRAVE* the antonym is *cowardly*, not *careful*. For *PRAISE* it is *criticise*, not *ignore* — ignoring is not the opposite of praising. Test each option by making a mini-sentence pair: 'He praised the plan / He criticised the plan' — clean contradiction.

**Skill 2 — build the flip.** Most adjectives flip with a prefix:

| Prefix | Effect | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| un- | not / reverse | unfair, unwell, undo, untie |
| in- / im- / il- / ir- | not | inactive, impossible, illogical, irregular |
| dis- | opposite, apart | disagree, disorder, disconnect, discredit |
| non- | not | nonsense, nonstop, nonviolent |
| mis- | wrongly | misjudge, misplace, misinterpret |
| de- | down, reverse | decrease, deflate, decompose |
| anti- | against | antisocial, antidote, antiseptic |
| counter- | against, opposite | counteract, counterclaim |
| -less | without | harmless, restless, speechless |
| -ful / -ous | full of (builds the positive) | harmful, dangerous, famous |

Prefix knowledge works in both directions: meet *irreversible*, know it means *reversible* negated; need the opposite of *conformity*, answer *nonconformity* or *defiance*. Watch the four-way *in- / im- / il- / ir-* spelling split — it follows the next sound (impossible, illegal, irregular) and decides spelling questions as a bonus.

**Antonym families to bank together:** agree/disagree, appear/disappear, increase/decrease, superior/inferior, permanent/temporary, expand/contract, vacant/occupied, sacred/profane, native/foreign, optimist/pessimist. SSC antonyms usually come straight from these families.

**Degree opposites:** gradable pairs sit on one line — hot↔cold, abundant↔scarce, shallow↔deep. Complementary pairs allow no middle — alive↔dead, guilty↔innocent. Both types appear; recognising the type prevents choosing a merely-different word.

tricks.title: Mini-sentence contradiction
tricks.body: Put the word and each candidate in the same short sentence ('The manager praised / criticised the report'). The option producing a genuine contradiction is the antonym.

example.q: Antonym of CORDIAL: warm / polite / hostile / sincere.
example.solution: 'A cordial welcome' ↔ 'a hostile welcome' — real opposites. 'Polite' and 'sincere' can coexist with cordial, so neither contradicts it.

tricks.title: Prefix flip check
tricks.body: Before scanning options, guess the flip yourself (conformity → nonconformity). If your guess is among the options, mark it — the options are built around the same flip.

tricks.title: Absence is not opposition
tricks.body: Kill options that merely lack the quality ('careful' for 'brave'). An antonym fights the word; it does not stand beside it.

mistakes: Choosing a word from a different part of speech ('arrive' as antonym of 'departure').
Taking a near-neutral word ('polite') as the opposite of a warm word ('cordial').
Opposing the wrong sense of a polysemous word ('fresh' = new vs unwilted; SSC picks the listed sense).

subtopics.title: Exam strategy for vocabulary questions
subtopics.concept:
Tier 1 typically carries only 1 synonym + 1 antonym, and Tier 2 a similar sprinkle — low volume, but each is a 15-second mark with none of grammar's ambiguity. The strategy is therefore about *conversion rate*, not time.

**The conversion system:**
- **Daily 15 minutes** on the word bank in this topic: 10 words a day, meanings read aloud, each used in one sentence of your own. Production, not recognition, fixes recall.
- **Weekly mixed test:** 30 random words from the bank — synonym for half, antonym for half. Target 26+.
- **PYQ mining:** note every vocabulary word from past papers into a personal sheet; the same words return within 2–4 years.
- **Root of the day:** one root and its five relatives. Forty days completes the root table.

**In the exam:** vocabulary items should take 15–20 seconds each. If a word is unknown, split it for roots; if still dark, judge its charge (+/−) from the shape and pick a matching-charge option — this beats random guessing. There is no negative marking on one skipped item's worth of time saved, but never leave an SSC vocabulary item blank: an educated 50-50 is positive expected value, and pure instinct in English correlates surprisingly well with correctness.

**Do not sacrifice** grammar or RC time for vocabulary — the return per minute is far higher there. Vocabulary is a background process: daily small doses, permanent retention.

tricks.title: Two-pass vocabulary
tricks.body: Answer every certain vocabulary item in the first pass (15 s each); in the second pass, return to unknowns and root-split them with the remaining time.

tricks.title: Charge guess with options
tricks.body: Options reveal the axis: if options are (kind, cruel, wealthy, talkative), the axis is temperament — now guess the word's charge from its sound (mal-, dys- negative; bene-, eu- positive) and pick accordingly.

tricks.title: The 2-4 year echo
tricks.body: Words repeat across years. Solving the last 5 years' synonym/antonym questions is the single highest-yield vocabulary exercise — the bank above already encodes that history.

mistakes: Cramming 500 words the night before; retention needs spaced daily doses.
Spending five minutes on one unknown word worth one mark.
Leaving vocabulary blank instead of making an educated charge-based choice.
Learning meanings without using the word in a sentence — recognition without recall.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A capitalised word with four options, stem asks the closest meaning.
pyqPatterns.approach: Say the meaning in your own words, then match overlap, degree and charge; split unknown words by root.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Same format, stem asks the word most opposite.
pyqPatterns.approach: Build the mini-sentence contradiction for each surviving option; try the prefix flip first.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Synonym/antonym of a word inside a phrase
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The word appears quoted from a short sentence or phrase ('gave up', 'broke out').
pyqPatterns.approach: Take the meaning from the phrase's usage first, then match options to that specific sense.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A blank whose options are near-synonyms differing in register or degree.
pyqPatterns.approach: Use the sentence's tone to pick the matching register and degree — the synonym skill in context.

solvedExamples.q:
Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.

BENEVOLENT
solvedExamples.solution: *Benevolent* = bene (good) + vol (wishing) = wishing others well → **compassionate**. The root instantly disposes of *malevolent* (male- = bad), which is its antonym and a planted decoy; *miserly* is about money and *talkative* about speech.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Split the word: bene- = good → pick the warm option; the male- option is the trap.

solvedExamples.q:
Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.

FRUGAL
solvedExamples.solution: *Frugal* means careful and sparing with money → **thrifty**. *Lavish* is its direct opposite (spending freely), and the other two are topic-shifters. Degree also confirms it: both 'frugal' and 'thrifty' sit at the same moderate mark of careful spending.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Meaning in your words ('spends carefully') → match, then check that the strongest-sounding option is not the antonym.

solvedExamples.q:
Select the word which is most opposite in meaning to the given word.

CORDIAL
solvedExamples.solution: *Cordial* = warm and friendly. The genuine contradiction is **hostile**. *Polite* and *sincere* both coexist with cordiality (a cordial host is also polite), so neither opposes it; *formal* describes style, not warmth.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Mini-sentence test: 'a cordial welcome' vs 'a ___ welcome' — only one option truly flips the meaning.

practice.q:
Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.

ABUNDANT
practice.solution: *Abundant* = existing in more than enough quantity → **plentiful**. *Scarce* is its antonym and is planted first-position bait; 'hidden' and 'tiny' shift to other dimensions altogether.
practice.shortcut: Own words first ('more than enough') → match.

practice.q:
Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.

FUTILE
practice.solution: *Futile* = producing no result → **pointless**. 'Useful' is the opposite pole; 'fertile' and 'fragile' share the -ile ending to punish shape-readers.
practice.shortcut: Kill same-suffix decoys, keep the meaning match.

practice.q:
Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.

IMMINENT
practice.solution: *Imminent* = about to happen at any moment → **impending**. 'Delayed/distant' push the event away in time — the opposite direction.
practice.shortcut: Time word: 'about to happen' → pick the option meaning 'on its way'.

practice.q:
Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.

NOTORIOUS
practice.solution: *Notorious* is famous **for bad reasons** → **infamous**. 'Renowned/celebrated/popular' all carry a positive charge — the charge mismatch is the entire test here.
practice.shortcut: Charge matching: a negative word needs a negative option.

practice.q:
Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.

INDISPENSABLE
practice.solution: *Indispensable* = too necessary to do without → **essential**. 'Optional' flips the meaning; the others shift axes. Prefix logic agrees: in- (not) + dispensable (able to be let go).
practice.shortcut: Prefix flip: not dispensable → must be kept → essential.

practice.q:
Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.

MITIGATE
practice.solution: *Mitigate* = soften the severity of something → **lessen**. *Aggravate* is the planted antonym; 'prolong' and 'conceal' change the action, not its intensity.
practice.shortcut: Root family: mit/miss (send) — 'send away the severity' → lessen.

practice.q:
Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.

VIGILANT
practice.solution: *Vigilant* = carefully watchful for danger → **alert**. 'Careless' and 'drowsy' are opposite-directed; 'hostile' shifts to temperament.

practice.q:
Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.

SQUANDER
practice.solution: *Squander* = spend or use carelessly → **waste**. 'Save' is its opposite; 'donate' is controlled giving, not waste; 'multiply' changes the direction entirely.

practice.q:
Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.

TENACIOUS
practice.solution: *Tenacious* = holding on firmly, refusing to quit → **persistent**. 'Fragile' and 'sluggish' are the planted opposite-temperament options.

practice.q:
Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.

LUCID
practice.solution: *Lucid* = easy to understand, transparent in expression → **clear**. 'Murky' is the opposite direction; 'lengthy/loud' are sound-shape decoys sharing the u-c sound.

practice.q:
Select the word which is most opposite in meaning to the given word.

HUMBLE
practice.solution: *Humble* = modest about one's worth. The genuine opposite is **proud**. 'Modest' is a synonym planted as bait; 'gentle/polite' describe manner, not self-regard.
practice.shortcut: Mini-sentence: 'a humble officer' vs 'a ___ officer' — only one option truly inverts it.

practice.q:
Select the word which is most opposite in meaning to the given word.

PUNCTUAL
practice.solution: *Punctual* = exactly on time. Its opposite is **late**. 'Early' is not the opposite — arriving early is still not punctual in the strict sense, and SSC's key follows 'late'; 'prompt/regular' are near-synonyms.
practice.shortcut: Time-axis test: on time ↔ behind time.

practice.q:
Select the word which is most opposite in meaning to the given word.

TRANSPARENT
practice.solution: *Transparent* = letting light through; its standard opposite is **opaque**. 'Visible/lucid' move in a different dimension; 'brittle' is physical weakness.
practice.shortcut: Physical sense here: see-through ↔ not see-through.

practice.q:
Select the word which is most opposite in meaning to the given word.

LIBERTY
practice.solution: *Liberty* = freedom from restraint → opposite **bondage**. 'Freedom' is the synonym bait; 'licence' is unrestrained permission, not captivity; 'leisure' is free time.
practice.shortcut: The synonym is always the first option to kill in antonym questions.

practice.q:
Select the word which is most opposite in meaning to the given word.

VIRTUE
practice.solution: *Virtue* = moral goodness → its standard opposite is **vice** (moral fault). 'Value' drifts to worth, and the v-initial 'virtuosity/vigour' are shape decoys.
practice.shortcut: Kill the v-initial decoys; pick the genuine moral opposite.
